Article Title: After Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees, CEO Satya Nadella explains the decision; says: I wish I could just sit here and ...
Article Text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella : ‘Vote with your feet’

What was Microsoft’s buyout offer

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has addressed the question over the tech giant’s massive new buyout program and whether this is a sign of upcoming AI-driven layoffs, explaining that the company is reshaping how its teams work rather than simply shrinking its headcount. Speaking after Microsoft rolled out a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to roughly 60,000 workers, which is more than a quarter of its global staff—Nadella emphasized that the future of the company will look noticeably different in terms of team sizes and daily workflows.“It’s a very important question. Let’s acknowledge that there is going to be plenty of opportunity going forward. The shape of that opportunity may be different,” Nadella said, adding, “The shape of what this new thing looks like is going to be different than what it was before: team sizes and team workflows.” While Nadella stressed that he wants all 200,000-plus Microsoft employees to grow and flourish, he noted that the workforce “will have to be configured in different ways. ”According to the CEO, the voluntary buyout is designed to give employees control over their careers as the company evolves, especially for those sitting in units that have been slow to adapt.“This voluntary thing was mostly about letting everybody have more agency to get themselves into places that make sense for their economic opportunity long term.That's, I think, the key thing. I don't want to be stuck in a team that's not transforming, even inside of Microsoft. Let's face it. It's not like I can sit here and say every part of Microsoft has really got the memo," Nadella explained at The Pragmatic Engineer podcast.He added that employees who feel professionally stuck now have the option to leave on good terms, though he encouraged them to explore internal transfers first.“If you're in a team where you feel stuck professionally, you can vote with your feet. I don't want you to, because quite frankly there are many places you can go inside of Microsoft itself. I wish I could just sit here and say it'll all be the same. I cannot. And this is one of those places where I want to be as transparent about the change,” Nadella said.Chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the Voluntary Exit Offer in a memo to staff, framing it as a chance for employees already considering a move outside Microsoft to exit now with financial backing and career support. The offer applies to eligible staff at internal level 70 and below, which is a group that includes roles up to general managers and some vice presidents, across just four countries: The US, Canada, The UK and India.Unlike Microsoft’s spring retirement buyout, this offer has no age or tenure minimums and job performance is not a factor. Eligible workers have until the first week of December to decide, with departures set for the end of the year.The buyout terms match Microsoft’s standard severance package. During US layoffs earlier this year, severance included at least 60 days of base pay on the payroll and up to 39 weeks of base pay depending on seniority and tenure – giving employees at level 64 and below one week of base pay per six months of service, and those at levels 65 to 67 two weeks per six months.The VEO also covers continued stock vesting, career transition help, and healthcare coverage for a fixed period. Unlike the earlier retirement program, however, it does not include extended healthcare benefits. Individual terms are being sent via email to eligible staff, including those in India.This marks Microsoft’s second major buyout push in 2026 following waves of layoffs over the past two years. In 2025 cuts, Microsoft eliminated more than 15,000 jobs.This year, the company launched its first-ever Voluntary Retirement Program for about 8,750 US staff (senior director level and below) whose age and years of service totaled at least 70. Microsoft laid off 4,800 workers (around 2% of its workforce) in July, hitting Xbox and commercial sales hardest, followed by hundreds more cuts in September.
Article Summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says the future of the company will look noticeably different in terms of team sizes and daily workflows. Microsoft rolled out a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to roughly 60,000 workers, which is more than a quarter of its global staff.

Article Title: A Melbourne woman spent A$2,000 on four Apple gift cards at Coles, but discovered their redemption codes were scratched out; the supermarket initially refused a refund before agreeing to return her mo
Article Text:
Image Credit: AI Generated

Melbourne woman's A$2,000 Apple gift cards found with scratched-out codes

Why did Coles initially refuse to refund the money

How did Coles eventually agree to return the A$2,000

What did the ABC investigation discover about gift card fraud

How does the gift card tampering scam operate

Are Australian supermarkets taking steps to prevent the problem

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A Melbourne woman who spent A$2,000 on four Apple gift cards at Coles discovered that their redemption codes had been scratched out, leaving her unable to use the vouchers. The purchase, which initially appeared to be a way to earn extra Flybuys points, turned into a frustrating dispute after supermarket staff reportedly refused to refund the money. The retailer eventually reversed its decision and agreed to return the amount. The incident later became part of a wider ABC News investigation into tampered gift cards being sold across Australia.According to an ABC News investigation report published on May 21, 2026, Melbourne-based illustrator Georgia Perry bought four Apple gift cards from a Coles supermarket in Yarraville, an inner-western suburb of Melbourne. Each card was worth A$500, bringing the total purchase to A$2,000.Perry had purchased the vouchers on a Tuesday evening because she wanted to buy a new iPhone. An in-store promotion offering 20 times the usual Flybuys points on Apple gift card purchases also made the deal appear attractive.However, the purchase took an unexpected turn when she returned home and began opening the cards. The first voucher appeared to have no usable redemption code, with the area where the code should have been showing signs of scratching or peeling.Initially, Perry thought she might have damaged it while removing the card from its packaging.The same problem appeared on the remaining three cards. All four vouchers had their redemption codes scratched out, making them unusable for the intended purchase.Perry took the four vouchers back to the supermarket after discovering the damage. However, she told ABC News that the store staff were unwilling to help and reportedly explained that they could not take responsibility because gift cards were third-party products.She also contacted Apple for assistance. During the process, the company's helpline asked her to provide photographs of the cards, including their serial numbers. This revealed another problem, as the final digits on the cards had also been scratched out.Perry subsequently lodged a formal complaint with Coles. The supermarket confirmed receiving it and said its customer care team had responded within an hour and continued working towards a resolution.The initial response left Perry dissatisfied. She described the customer service experience as uninterested and lacking urgency. She also questioned how the cards could have reached the shop floor in that condition, particularly because the damage was not obvious while they remained attached to their cardboard packaging.The situation changed after Perry shared a video of her experience on Instagram. Her complaint attracted widespread attention, receiving more than 150,000 views by the morning after it was posted, alongside hundreds of comments from people discussing gift card fraud and consumer rights.According to ABC News, a Coles employee left Perry a voicemail confirming that a refund would be issued. Emails reviewed by the ABC team showed that the gift card supplier had deactivated the A$2,000 worth of vouchers and returned the money to Coles.The supermarket subsequently informed Perry that she was eligible for a refund and apologised for the poor experience.In an extensive investigation published on August 31, 2026, ABC News revealed that shoppers across Australia had reported buying gift cards with missing or damaged redemption codes from major supermarket chains.The investigation examined 19 reports of suspicious gift cards, many involving Apple vouchers. It reviewed customer receipts, photographs of damaged cards and correspondence with retailers, Apple and gift card distributors.The earliest reports identified by the ABC dated back to 2024. That year, a Coles customer in Perth and a Woolworths shopper in Sydney reported problems with their purchases.The ABC investigation identified another customer, Lavkesh Arora, who bought five Apple gift cards worth A$2,000 from a Coles store in the city’s eastern suburbs. Two of the cards worth A$700 combined, had missing redemption codes and digits. Another shopper, Damian Toohey, reported finding a scratched-off number on an Apple gift card purchased from Woolworths.The ABC investigation also examined how criminals could tamper with physical gift cards before returning them to supermarket shelves.Adam Parks, a former Australian representative of the US Department of Homeland Security's investigative unit, explained that the practice is commonly known in the industry as card draining.According to Parks, the process can involve people taking gift cards from shop shelves, carefully opening their packaging and recording the information needed to access the funds. They may use razor blades or hair dryers to remove the packaging without leaving obvious signs of damage.The cards are then returned to their packaging and placed back on supermarket shelves. When an unsuspecting customer purchases one, the retailer activates it at the checkout.The stolen information can then be used to monitor the card's balance and activation status. Once a customer pays for the voucher, those involved in the scam may spend its value before the buyer gets an opportunity to redeem it.This can make the fraud difficult to identify immediately. Gift cards are frequently purchased as presents, meaning some customers might not open them for weeks or months after the original transaction.Parks told ABC News that the operation becomes profitable when carried out on a large scale, with different people potentially handling the collection, tampering and use of the stolen information.The ABC investigation found that Coles had previously worked with police to address gift card tampering. Court documents revealed that a man was arrested after allegedly placing tampered Apple gift cards on shelves on at least 5 Coles stores in Sydney.Police alleged that the cards involved were worth at least A$10,200. The man was sentenced to a two-year community corrections order and a 15-month suspended sentence.Both Coles and Woolworths acknowledged the wider problem and defended their efforts to prevent it. Woolworths was trialling anti-tamper hangers and staffed stations near gift card displays in some stores.Apple had also changed its Australian gift card packaging in early 2025. The newer design included perforated edges intended to make signs of opening or interference easier to identify. Its packaging also carried a warning against buying or selling cards that appeared to have been tampered with.
Article Summary: Melbourne woman's A$2,000 Apple gift cards found with scratched-out codes. Coles initially refused to refund the money. The retailer eventually reversed its decision and agreed to return the amount. Incident later became part of a wider ABC News investigation into tampered gift cards being sold across Australia.

Article Title: Argos denied a customer in UK refund for a $500 laptop bought online, as had switched it on and activated Windows 11; two years later, he won a Court of Appeal ruling as the court upheld 'sealed-softw
Article Text:
AI generated image for representation

Why did Argos refuse the refund at first

What does the sealed-software exception cover

Can retailers still deduct money for use

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Argos has been ordered to refund a customer who activated Windows 11 on his laptop. The Court of Appeal in England and Wales has ruled that switching on a computer bought online and activating its pre-installed operating system to test it does not, by itself, remove the buyer’s statutory cancellation right.According to a report by Solicitor News, the unanimous ruling rejected Argos’s reliance on the “sealed-software exception” after Dr Ebenezer Adodo sought to return a $500 Lenovo laptop in September 2024. The court held that he had bought a computer with an operating system installed, rather than sealed software sold separately. It ordered Argos to refund the price with interest, clarifying the distinction between testing an online purchase and using goods beyond what is necessary to assess them.Adodo ordered the Lenovo IdeaPad, preloaded with Windows 11, through Argos’s website on August 31, 2024. He also bought a $13 mouse pad and collected both items that day.At home, he switched on the laptop to check whether it met his needs. He found compatibility problems with software he used for his work at Leicester University. The mouse pad was also too large for his computer table.He repacked both products and took them back on September 5.Argos refused the return, citing opened packaging and the laptop having been switched on.An initial county court decision accepted Argos’s argument that the purchase was not a distance contract. On appeal, a judge found that the contract had been concluded online and awarded a refund for the mouse pad. However, that judge accepted that activating Windows 11 had broken a digital seal, preventing cancellation of the laptop purchase. Adodo then took the laptop dispute to the Court of Appeal.The Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 generally allow consumers to cancel an online goods purchase within 14 days of receiving it, without giving a reason.An exception covers sealed computer software that becomes unsealed after delivery. The appeal court interpreted that exception narrowly: the software must itself be the object of the sale, supplied on a physically sealed carrier such as a CD or USB stick.A laptop’s pre-installed operating system did not turn the computer purchase into that kind of software transaction. Activating Windows to assess the machine therefore did not extinguish Adodo’s cancellation right.The ruling does not give buyers unrestricted use of a product before returning it. Regulation 34 allows retailers to recover a proven reduction in value caused by handling beyond what is necessary to establish the goods’ nature, characteristics and functioning.Reasonable resetting costs may qualify in an appropriate case. However, Argos had not established whether such costs existed or how much they were. The court ordered interest on the laptop refund from 14 days after Adodo’s unsuccessful return attempt.
Article Summary: Dr Ebenezer Adodo tried to return a $500 Lenovo laptop in September 2024. Argos refused the return, citing opened packaging and the laptop having been switched on. The Court of Appeal in England and Wales has ruled that switching on a computer bought online and activating its pre-installed operating system does not, by itself, remove the buyer’s statutory cancellation right.

Article Title: Microsoft 365 outage: Company blames a 'triple' failure for 24-hour-plus global Outlook disruption; Microsoft EVP Charles Lamanna says: Three main factors that...
Article Text:
Microsoft explains its global outage

A July bug slipped past Microsoft 365's load testing

A Teams failover and 14% missing capacity exposed the bug

Outlook stayed down longest because Exchange Online could not switch gateways

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft has explained what disrupted Outlook, Exchange Online and a string of other Microsoft 365 services for more than 24 hours last week, and the answer is not one fault but three. A software bug that had sat unnoticed on its servers since July, a sudden rise in traffic and a chunk of server capacity already offline all lined up on November 12. The result was a chain reaction that left more than 80% of the servers behind a key Microsoft 365 networking gateway unresponsive at the worst point.Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, detailed the root cause of the Microsoft 365 outage in a post on X on Monday. "The incident on Thursday, November 12th, 2026, was caused by three main factors that together caused a global outage for the networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services," he wrote. He also apologised: "We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations. "The first factor was a latent defect. Under certain load conditions, lock contention inside an internal process left servers overwhelmed and unresponsive.The bug came from a fix built specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Lamanna said neither the defect nor that fix applies to broader Windows deployments.The change began rolling out in July, cleared safe deployment, reached servers worldwide over several weeks and ran for more than three months without trouble.So why did testing miss it? Microsoft's load tests leaned on its weaker hardware with fewer cores, while the contention problem gets worse on newer machines with more cores. The test labs' traffic and hardware mix did not match the live fleet.Microsoft runs two independent network gateway systems inside Microsoft 365, so services can move between them during disruptions. About 15 hours before the outage, Teams failed over from the alternative gateway to the "primary" one, which also handles Exchange Online. The company calls this routine, but it added load and changed traffic patterns on that gateway.At the same time, nearly 14% of the gateway's server capacity was out of service because of an unrelated issue from the day before. That alone caused no harm, since the service had enough headroom.Together, though, the extra load and thinner capacity triggered the July bug during peak US traffic hours. Requests piled up until servers stopped responding. Microsoft's traffic management then moved users to healthy endpoints, as designed, which simply spread the same load across fewer machines. In under two hours, the defect had hit servers across the fleet.A separate issue meant the bulkheads between regional "capacity units" also failed to contain the damage, letting a gateway problem become a global outage.Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps could move off the faulty infrastructure, which is why they came back sooner. Teams chats and meetings worked for most of the outage. Exchange Online, which powers Outlook email, could not make that switch.Recovery was a fight of its own. Servers returning to service were flooded by queued traffic and went down again. Microsoft's automated recovery systems were not designed for such a broad failure, and because the bug was months old, the usual rollback, flighting and feature flag tools could not quickly reverse it. Even the company's status updates during the outage said it had "not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact.Engineers eventually built an update that returned the code path to its last known good state. They then pulled groups of servers out of service, applied the fix and restarted them, in some cases more than half a region at a time.Microsoft first flagged the problem at 11:24 pm IST on November 12, for users in the Americas, before it spread to at least 70 countries and hit Copilot, government offices, courts and hospitals. In India, IndiGo and Akasa Air reported problems with their customer-support email systems, while OpenAI and Anthropic flagged issues with their Microsoft 365 integrations. The Microsoft executive had already ruled out foul play on November 13, writing, "This was not a cyberattack or an issue caused by AI tooling. "A final Post-Incident Review (PIR) is due later this week. It should also shed light on the separate issue that let the failure jump across regions, which Monday's summary leaves unexplained.
Article Summary: Microsoft 365 went down for more than 24 hours on November 12. A software bug that had sat unnoticed on its servers since July, a sudden rise in traffic and a chunk of server capacity already offline all lined up. The result was a chain reaction that left more than 80% of the servers behind a key Microsoft 365 networking gateway unresponsive.

Article Title: US expands 'China ban' on Nvidia chips to 12 other countries: Here's the full list and what it means
Article Text:
' China ban ' on Nvidia chips: What the new restrictions mean

Five countries named

Exemptions

Markets react; Nvidia shares fall

Pressure on Commerce Department grows

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Countries affected by the proposed rule

The US Commerce Department has now unveiled new restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese companies and other US adversaries from accessing advanced artificial intelligence computing power through overseas data centers, according to Bloomberg report. Under an interim rule release on November 16, the datacenter operators in counties including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil will be required to obtain a US government licence before purchasing advanced AI chips from manufacturers such as Nvidia. The measure is designed to prevent companies from bypassing existing export controls through remote access to computing infrastructure located outside China.“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Commerce Department said in a statement.This move of the US Commerce Department highlights the growing US concerns that advanced cloud-computing networks have made it easier for Chinese entities to remotely tap into powerful AI systems powered by US-designed semiconductors, even when they cannot directly import the chips themselves.By extending licensing requirements to a wider group of countries, Washington is seeking to align rules governing remote access with existing restrictions on the physical shipment of advanced AI hardware. Under the proposal, licence applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.The rule requires licences to export, re-export or transfer advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. Licences will be considered case by case, and the rule describes these countries as presenting a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” The department said the rule is meant to ensure that existing restrictions on sensitive American technology “cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries. ”The rule exempts US-headquartered companies operating in the listed countries, which can keep shipping AI chips there without a licence. It also exempts shipments to data centers used as commercial recommender systems for online retailers or social media companies. The draft rule takes effect once it is published in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of 9 am Monday, Bloomberg reported.Nvidia shares fell as much as 2.9% on the news, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped as much as 5.5%. The restrictions apply not only to Nvidia but also to other US companies that manufacture advanced AI processors.The draft rule arrives amid heightened scrutiny of US export-control enforcement following allegations involving Nvidia and Singapore-based Megaspeed International. According to the Bloomberg report, the Commerce Department and senior officials, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, have faced increasing criticism over their handling of export-control programmes. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently suggested that the Commerce Department had not acted quickly enough to tighten restrictions."As I said, many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen," Bessent said during an appearance on Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures, according to Bloomberg. The Commerce Department's statement announcing the new rule said it was written "by and at the direction" of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, indicating broad support within the administration for tougher controls.According to the Bloomberg report, the new licensing requirements would apply to data-centre operators in 12 countries:* Singapore* Malaysia* Thailand* Indonesia* Brazil* Mexico* Philippines* Vietnam* India* South Africa* Saudi Arabia* United Arab EmiratesThe countries listed above have become an important hub for AI infrastructure, cloud-computing facilities and semiconductor-related investments. These are the reasons why US is making them a focal point in order to control the access of advanced AI technologies.
Article Summary: New restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese companies from accessing advanced artificial intelligence computing power through overseas data centers. Datacenter operators in counties including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil will be required to obtain a US government licence. The measure is designed to prevent companies from bypassing existing export controls through remote access.

Article Title: Canada faces pushback from Meta, Apple, Alphabet and Signal over Canadian bill that could force them to weaken encryption
Article Text:
Why tech companies are threatening to leave Canada

The ‘fight’ over encryption and ‘backdoors’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is reportedly running into fierce resistance from major technology companies over proposed security legislation that would force digital platforms to retain and hand over user data to law enforcement. Executives and lobbyists from Facebook-parent Meta, Apple , and Google-parent Alphabet said to be leading a last-ditch push in Ottawa to rewrite the legislation before it becomes law. Leaders from Meta, Signal Messenger and Tailscale are set to take their objections directly to a key Canadian Senate committee hearing that will shape the bill’s final text, Bloomberg reported.Known as Bill C-22, the “lawful access” legislation is designed to let Canada’s police services and spy agency require electronic service providers to preserve and turn over specific metadata. While the Canadian government argues the rules simply bring the country in line with its Five Eyes and Group of Seven (G7) allies, tech companies, privacy advocates, and US lawmakers contend the bill goes much further – putting user privacy and platform security at risk.Meta has warned that the legislation would effectively turn its platforms into “an arm of the government’s surveillance apparatus.” “There’s a real possibility that both the security and the privacy of Canadian users of these systems is really undermined,” Rachel Curran, Meta’s head of public policy in Canada, said in an interview, the publication reported.For Carney’s government, the standoff carries real economic and diplomatic risks, including chilling tech investment, straining relations with the US and pushing privacy-focused services out of the country altogether. Signal has threatened to pull out of the Canadian market if Bill C-22 passes in its current form while Proton AG, a Swiss tech firm, has said it would reconsider its expansion plans in Canada.Critics take particular issue with a provision allowing authorities to force service providers to store certain user metadata for up to six months in case law enforcement requests it.Bill C-22 could also require certain companies to unlock encrypted data – though only if the company built the encryption itself and holds the keys needed to unlock it. Earlier this year, lawmakers amended the bill to clarify that firms cannot be forced to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their software.Those safeguards were meant to reassure companies like Signal and Meta (which owns WhatsApp) that end-to-end encryption wouldn’t be targeted. Because end-to-end encryption ensures only the sender and recipient can read a message, the companies themselves have no way to decrypt the content.Still, privacy groups and tech leaders argue the bill leaves the government with broad authority to order firms to build “technical capabilities” to intercept communications and hand over data. Tech companies have consistently maintained that they cannot build a law enforcement “backdoor” without weakening security for everyone.Curran called any order that weakens Meta’s systems a “red line” for the company and likely its peers. “It probably puts Canada in a position where there’s going to eventually be a bit of a standoff between service providers and the government, and it’s not good for Canadians,” she added.Meanwhile, Canada’s public safety minister Gary Anandasangaree has maintained that Bill C-22 was already revised to address the encryption concerns, accusing Big Tech critics of spreading misinformation.“Bill C-22 does not authorise indiscriminate surveillance and does not permit or compel companies to introduce systemic vulnerabilities or so-called ‘backdoors.’ Any claims suggesting otherwise are incorrect,” said Simon Lafortune, the minister’s spokesperson, in a statement.Apple has acknowledged the government’s efforts to improve the draft, but said the current bill would still hurt its ability to protect users with encryption and privacy tools, “even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses.”
Article Summary: Canadian government running into fierce resistance over proposed security legislation. Bill C-22 would force digital platforms to retain and hand over user data to law enforcement. Meta, Signal Messenger and Tailscale are set to take their objections directly to a key Canadian Senate committee hearing that will shape the bill’s final text.

Article Title: US government's Department of Commerce and Department of Justice ‘break rule’, issue joint statement on MegaSpeed, the company at 'centre' of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's 'romantic scandal'
Article Text:
Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice's joint statement on investigation into Singaporean company Megaspeed

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For the first time, two US government departments -- US Department of Commerce and Department of Justice -- have issued a joint statement on MegaSpeed, the Singapore-based company caught in Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's scandal. The statement makes it clear what made the two departments break the rule of not commenting on and ongoing investigations. The statement says, "While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting."For those unaware, the Singapore-based cloud computing company MegaSpeed has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12 amid fallout from reports about his extramarital relationships, one of which was reportedly a direct reportee.On its website, Megaspeed describes itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia’s computing power cloud business in the region. It enables customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs. The company has offices in Singapore and Indonesia.The Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice are providing the public with an update on the investigation of the Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has attracted significant public attention in the last week.While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting.After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang.Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred. This investigation is the result of the excellent work of the Department of Commerce under Secretary Howard Lutnick and the law enforcement efforts of the Department of Justice under Attorney General Todd Blanche.The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice. Under the Trump Administration, seventeen defendants across six separate investigations have been charged in connection with allegations of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of semiconductors. Furthermore, the Department of Commerce has brought monetary penalties to new highs across export control cases, representing an eighteen-fold increase over the Biden administration.Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America’s technological edge.
Article Summary: US Department of Commerce and Department of Justice have issued a joint statement on MegaSpeed, the Singapore-based company caught in Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's scandal. The statement says, "While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts"

Article Title: EY India opens registrations for sixth Board Effectiveness programme with focus on AI, cybersecurity
Article Text:
Boards expected to play a bigger strategic role

Focus on governance, technology and risk oversight

More than 40 hours of learning

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Wider leadership participation

EY India has announced the sixth cohort of its Executive Program on Board Effectiveness, aimed at equipping current directors and senior executives with the skills needed to navigate evolving boardroom responsibilities, including oversight of artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity and corporate governance. The four-week programme will commence on 19 November 2026 and is designed for existing board members as well as senior leaders aspiring to take up board positions. According to EY India, the initiative seeks to strengthen participants' strategic judgment, financial oversight and governance capabilities as expectations from corporate boards continue to expand beyond traditional compliance functions.EY India highlighted that directors are increasingly expected to contribute to strategy formation, risk governance, technology oversight, financial resilience and long-term value creation, rather than serving solely as compliance watchdogs. The firm cited findings from the ISB Corporate Governance Report 2025, which surveyed more than 200 directors from BSE 500 companies. While 98% of respondents said their boards were compliant with governance requirements, only 17% reported that their boards actively shaped company strategy. A further 36% said their boards had limited or no involvement beyond reviewing management plans.Commenting on the programme, Aashish Kasad, Partner and India Region Diversity & Inclusiveness Business Sponsor at EY India, said the transition from executive leadership to the boardroom requires a shift from operating a business to challenging, guiding and overseeing it."Directors need to connect strategy with financial resilience, governance and deliberate on organisation readiness on topical matters such as impact of AI and cybersecurity, while exercising independent judgment," Kasad said, adding that the programme is intended to help leaders contribute to boards with greater clarity and confidence.The Executive Program on Board Effectiveness includes more than 40 hours of learning across nine sessions. Topics covered include board leadership and effectiveness, directors' responsibilities, board committees, environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues, financial statement interpretation, AI and cybersecurity, board recruitment and emerging governance challenges. Participants will also engage in governance case studies, simulated board and committee discussions, and scenario-based exercises designed to enhance strategic contribution, risk awareness, stakeholder stewardship, integrity and ethical decision-making.Originally introduced as a platform for senior women leaders, the programme has now been expanded to a broader leadership audience. EY India said it plans to offer two cohorts each year, enabling more professionals to prepare for boardroom responsibilities and benefit from peer learning opportunities. The programme is targeted at CXO-level executives seeking board positions, senior leaders from corporate, public and non-profit organisations, investor representatives serving on boards, leaders from multinational companies and Indian subsidiaries, as well as existing directors looking to strengthen their effectiveness in a rapidly changing governance environment.
Article Summary: EY India has announced the sixth cohort of its Executive Program on Board Effectiveness. The four-week programme will commence on 19 November 2026 and is designed for existing board members as well as senior leaders aspiring to take up board positions. EY India said it plans to offer two cohorts each year, enabling more professionals to prepare for boardroom responsibilities.

Article Title: In September 2025, Larry Ellison briefly became world's richest man after OpenAI signed $300 billion deal with Oracle; 14 months later, he has lost $145 billion and why reason is again Sam Altman
Article Text:
How Oracle’s rally lifted Larry Ellison above Elon Musk

Why OpenAI has become a concern

Data-centre spending adds pressure despite revenue growth

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Larry Ellison’s net worth has fallen substantially as Oracle’s shares have dropped sharply since last year. Fourteen months after an AI-driven rally briefly made him the world’s richest person after the company signed a $300 billion deal with ChatGPT-maker OpenAI . Since then, the Oracle co-founder has reportedly lost an estimated $145 billion from his highest net worth. Concerns about Oracle’s reliance on Sam Altman-led OpenAI are part of the pressure on its stock, a report claims.In September 2025, OpenAI had agreed to purchase $300 billion in computing services from Oracle over roughly five years. That business helped fuel optimism about Oracle’s cloud expansion. Now, the scale of its commitment to one customer, alongside the cost of building data centres, has become a concern for investors, The Motley Fool reports.Oracle stock jumped for strong AI contracts and meeting growth expectations on September 10, 2025. At one point, the jump placed Ellison ahead of Elon Musk in Bloomberg’s Billionaire Index. However, by the end of the business day, Musk had regained his lead.Ellison’s brief tenure illustrated how closely his reported net worth tracked the market value of his Oracle stock. Likewise, the reported $145 billion fall reflects a drop in estimated wealth as share prices fell, not an equivalent cash payment or realised loss.Oracle reported a backlog of $664 billion at the end of its first fiscal quarter of 2026-2027. This represents contracted products and services that have not yet been delivered or recorded as revenue.The Motley Fool report estimates that at least $300 billion of that backlog comes from OpenAI, which is roughly 45% of the total. Such concentration leaves Oracle exposed if a major customer reduces spending or cannot meet its commitments.The contracts’ detailed terms are not public. The analysis shows a risk to future revenue; however, it does not establish that OpenAI has cancelled its orders.But Oracle’s operating results have kept climbing. Revenue for the quarter ended August 31, 2026, increased 30% to $19.3 billion and cloud revenue grew 62% to $11.6 billion. Investment in infrastructure used up more cash than the operations produced. We had about $23 billion in operating cash flow, and we had about $5 billion in negative free cash flow.Free cash flow measures cash remaining after capital investment, including spending on data centres and equipment. Oracle also disclosed selling $20 billion of common stock during the quarter to help fund its investment programme. Its challenge is turning contracted demand into revenue while financing the infrastructure needed to deliver it.
Article Summary: Oracle co-founder has reportedly lost an estimated $145 billion from his highest net worth. Concerns about Oracle’s reliance on Sam Altman-led OpenAI are part of the pressure on its stock, a report claims. OpenAI had agreed to purchase $300 billion in computing services from Oracle over roughly five years.

Article Title: Microsoft confirms a key detail of Xbox Project Helix, gaming unit's 25th anniversary magazine says it is a …
Article Text:
Project Helix: Console first, not a PC

‘Xbox is tackling rising hardware costs through new tech’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft has shared its clearest look yet at Project Helix, confirming details about its next-generation hardware. The details arrived through a publication of the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine, released as part of Microsoft’s celebrations marking 25 years of Xbox. While Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has previously referred to Project Helix as a “family of devices,” vice president of next generation Jason Ronald used the magazine feature to explain what that actually looks like for players: “designed to be a console capable of playing games from your PC.”Although Microsoft still hasn’t revealed what the physical hardware looks like, or confirmed speculation that it could arrive as soon as late 2027, Ronald stressed that Project Helix is rooted in the traditional console experience, even as it bridges the gap with PC gaming, the magazine says (via IGN).“We're very clear on the design goal: Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games,” Ronald said. He explained that the priority is making game access effortless and instant. At the same time, hardcore gamers and power users who want deeper customisation over graphics settings and performance options will still have the freedom to tweak them.According to Ronald, Project Helix is built to eliminate the walls that have historically separated gaming platforms: First is that players will be able to bring four generations of their Xbox game library and save progression with them instantly. The second is that the system removes what Ronald called “arbitrary constraints between console and PC games.”Reflecting on the past, Ronald admitted Microsoft “lost sight of what is truly magical” during the Xbox One era, promising that the future of Xbox is focused squarely on players, developers, and the games they love.One of the biggest questions hanging over next-gen hardware is price. The gaming industry is currently dealing with a component crisis that has pushed up the cost of consoles and storage, leaving many gamers dreading the price tags of upcoming machines.Ronald acknowledged the tough market, calling it a “challenging time,” but said the pressure has actually pushed his engineering team to innovate so Project Helix remains both cutting-edge and affordable.“This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering, because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower, additional memory, and things like that,” Ronald explained, adding, “I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last 10 years.”The magazine describes Project Helix as the “crown jewel in a platform able to move with you.” Whether someone is playing on a large living room TV, streaming to a small handheld screen, or sitting at a PC with a mouse and keyboard, Ronald wants the interface to feel distinctly “Xbox” while naturally adapting to each screen's strengths.
Article Summary: Project Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games, says Xbox vice president Jason Ronald. Project Helix could arrive as soon as late 2027.

Article Title: Apple Watch off, Fitbit Air on, and what’s easy to forget and what isn’t
Article Text:
The tracker that never comes off

I stopped taking it off, mostly because I forgot it was there

The coach talks a lot, and I've started listening

On a run, all that quiet starts working against me

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

I don't need a screen back, just a buzz now and then

About a kilometre into a run last week, I turned my wrist to check my pace and found myself looking at a blue fabric strap. I knew there was nothing on it, since I'd put it on myself that morning, but I still looked down twice more before I gave up, slowed to a jog and pulled my phone out of my pocket.That strap is Google 's Fitbit Air, and it's been on my wrist in place of my Apple Watch for the last few weeks. There's no screen on it and no buttons. A small sensor pod sits inside the fabric, keeps track of my heart rate, sleep, steps and workouts, and quietly sends all of it to the Google Health app on my phone. You're not meant to look at it at all, and for most of the day, I don't.Which is a bit odd, because running wasn't why it ended up on my wrist.For years, my Apple Watch spent every night on the bedside table. I'd kept the screen free of scratches since the day I got it, and the thought of banging it against the bed frame at 3am was enough to make me take it off before I slept, every single night. I never minded much, until I started running and wanted to know why some mornings my legs felt fresh and others felt heavy from the first step.The first night with the Air, I lay down half expecting to feel it on my wrist.I didn't. All that faces out is fabric, and the whole thing weighs around 12g with the band, so there was nothing to notice and nothing to protect. For the first time in years, I fell asleep with something on my wrist and didn't think about it once. The next morning, Google Health had a full night of sleep waiting for me, with a sleep score, heart rate variability and something called readiness, which I'd never had a reason to look at before.A couple of days later, I looked down in the middle of the afternoon to check whether I'd even put it on. It had been on since the night before. It only comes off when it needs charging, which so far has been about once a week.Those numbers would have meant very little to me on their own, and that's where Google's Gemini-powered Health Coach comes in. It lives in the app, and it has a lot to say.My mornings now start with it, usually before I've even got out of bed. I open the app to see how I slept, and the coach gives me a summary that runs longer than it needs to, then asks me something. How did I feel after yesterday's run? Did I sleep later than usual? I reply, and it asks something else. More than once, I've realised I've spent five minutes chatting with a tracker whose whole pitch is that I'll spend less time looking at screens.But it's also the first time anything has told me what my numbers mean for the day ahead. One morning, after a short night and a hard run the evening before, it said my readiness was low and suggested I go easy. On the Watch, I'd have seen a few numbers, not known what to make of them, and gone out anyway. This time, I swapped the run for a walk, and the run the day after felt a lot better.We've settled into a bit of a back and forth since then. It sets weekly goals based on how I've actually been doing, and when it asked for more runs than I thought I could manage at this stage, I said so and it eased off. The coach comes with Google Health Premium, which is free for the first three months and Rs 499 a month after that. The band costs Rs 13,999, and the basic tracking is free regardless. I'm still in my free months, and the coach is the one part I can see myself paying for.So, back to that run.I'm still new to running, and I haven't figured out pacing yet. I go out too fast more often than not, and I usually only realise it when I'm already out of breath. The Watch was how I kept myself in check. A glance told me my pace, distance and heart rate, and I'd push or ease off based on that.So on a run with the Air, my phone has to do that job. My AirPods Pro are in, playing whatever high-BPM playlist I've picked for the day, with noise cancellation off because I want to hear the traffic behind me on a Delhi road. Every time I want to know my pace, I have to slow down, pull the phone out, unlock it with sweaty fingers and find the workout screen, all while watching out for potholes, parked scooters and autos that seem to pull out the second I look down. By the time I've read the number and put the phone back, the rhythm I'd built up is gone. Once, a scooter swung out of a lane just as I was squinting at the screen, and I had to stop dead in the middle of the run to let it pass.I tried turning on audio updates, where the app reads out your stats every few minutes. They work, but they cut right across whatever song is playing, often just as it's getting good, and with the honking around me, I catch maybe half of what's said. More often than not, it's the half with the number I wanted.There's no getting around taking the phone, either. The Air doesn't have GPS, so for proper distance and a route map, it leans on the phone. Without it, the band guesses distance from steps, which is fine for a walk but not for someone trying to keep track of every kilometre.What gets to me is that the Air can already get my attention. It has a vibration motor, which it uses for silent alarms and low-battery alerts. If it buzzed once at every kilometre, or twice when I'd hit a goal the coach set, I'd barely need the phone on most runs. That feels like something a software update could sort out, and I hope Google is working on it.I get why it's this quiet the rest of the time. I don't want my wrist buzzing for every WhatsApp message or email, and a band like this shouldn't turn into a smartwatch. A run is the one time I want it to speak up.It's a bit funny when I think about it. The screen I was so careful with is the reason the Watch never stayed on overnight, and not having one is why the Air has been on my wrist every night for weeks. It's also why, a kilometre into a run, I'm still turning my wrist to look at a strap with nothing on it. For now, that’s a trade I’m happy to keep making, at least until my pace stops needing so much checking.
Article Summary: The Fitbit Air has no screen and no buttons. A small sensor pod sits inside the fabric, keeps track of my heart rate, sleep, steps and workouts, and quietly sends all of it to the Google Health app. It only comes off when it needs charging, which so far has been about once a week.

Article Title: Nyayadhi makes chat-based AI tool for legal research available to more users in India: Here’s how it will help lawyers
Article Text:
How can Nyayadhi help lawyers

“Legal research demands a higher standard than general-purpose AI.

A legal argument in a judgment is not the same as the courts’ findings, and a popular case is not necessarily the right precedent. Nyayadhi is designed to help lawyers distinguish between the two by bringing them closer to the pertinent judicial reasoning.”,

What does its accuracy claim mean

“Lawyers cannot work on approximations. Every

legal research

must be traceable to its source. Our zero-hallucination approach is built to earn lawyers’ trust and eliminate the scepticism that is prevalent around generic AI tools”,

Nyayadhi has opened its AI legal research tool for beta testing. The chat-based platform is aimed at advocates, law firms, in-house legal teams and other legal professionals in India. According to the company, it provides access to more than 50 lakh case documents from the Supreme Court, 15 High Courts, the National Company Law Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal.The platform is designed to help lawyers identify relevant judgments, examine the reasoning behind court decisions and prepare briefs. Nyayadhi says it uses AI to extract and summarise information from legal documents, with responses grounded in verifiable sources. The beta release follows an earlier pilot involving legal professionals.The beta version of the tool is available to legal professionals through Nyayadhi’s company website. The company did not specify pricing, the duration of beta access or a date for a wider commercial release.Rather than returning broad search results alone, Nyayadhi says its platform helps users locate judgments containing judicial reasoning relevant to their research.It was developed in collaboration with practising lawyers with more than 65 years of combined experience across legal domains.Its extraction and summarisation tools are intended to support case law analysis and brief preparation. The company positions these features as research support for drafting, advising clients and presenting cases.said Achal Gupta, Partner-Disputes/Litigation, CKM Partners.Nyayadhi describes its system as following a zero-hallucination approach. In AI, hallucinations refer to incorrect or invented information presented as factual. The company says its approach grounds outputs in verifiable legal sources rather than unverified generated content.said Prasenjit Moitra, Co-founder, Nyayadhi.The company did not provide an independent accuracy assessment or detailed test results supporting that claim. It says pilot users found the platform more useful than conventional search methods for extracting specific information, but does not disclose the number of participants or evaluation criteria.

The chat-based platform is aimed at advocates, law firms, in-house legal teams and other legal professionals in India. The platform is designed to help lawyers identify relevant judgments, examine the reasoning behind court decisions and prepare briefs.

Article Title: Microsoft's top AI executive says ‘deeply sorry' for outage, shares three causes for disruption
Article Text:
Microsoft global outage

Three causes of Microsoft 365 services’ global outage

Cause 1: A hidden defect

in the servers

Cause 2: A surge in load

Cause 3: Reduced server capacity

How the Microsoft 365 services outage spread

Why some services came back sooner

Why recovery took longer than usual

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft has apologised for a global outage that hit its Microsoft 365 services last week and has explained what went wrong. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, shared the company’s Preliminary Post-Incident Report on the outage that took place last week. The incident happened on Thursday, November 12, 2026. According to Microsoft, three main factors came together to cause a global outage of the networking gateway that sits in front of many Microsoft 365 services. More details on the root cause are available in the Microsoft 365 Admin center, and Lamanna shared a shorter version.“More details on the root cause can be found in the Microsoft 365 Admin center, and an abridged version can be found below. We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” Lamanna said.According to the Microsoft executive, three primary issues converged to knock offline the networking gateway that underpins several Microsoft 365 services.The first cause was a latent defect. Under certain load conditions, it left servers overwhelmed and unresponsive.Microsoft said the problem was lock contention inside an internal process, which made the machine unavailable. The defect came from a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Microsoft said neither the defect nor the fix applies to broader Windows deployments.The change first began rolling out in July this year. It went through safe deployment and spread globally over several weeks, and no issues were seen. For more than three months, the change ran worldwide without any impact.The second cause was a surge in load, which made it more likely that the gateways would run into the contention. Microsoft 365 uses two independent and heterogeneous network gateway systems, built for isolation and high availability. This allows many services to fail over between them during outages or disruptions.About fifteen hours before the outage, Teams failed over from the alternative gateway to the “primary” gateway, which also supports Exchange Online. That increased the load on the primary gateway and changed its traffic patterns. Microsoft said this kind of failover is part of normal operations and is an integral part of its standard resiliency efforts.The third cause was that nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was out of service at the same time. The cause was an unrelated issue from the previous day. The capacity was on track to return to service through routine maintenance and health processes.Microsoft said the higher load and the lower server capacity together caused the gateway to hit the latent bug from July. Requests built up until the servers stopped responding. This happened during the peak window of traffic in the United States.When servers lose connectivity, Microsoft’s traffic management systems automatically send users to other healthy endpoints. This happens often and normally keeps the service resilient. This time, however, the redirected traffic raised the chance of the same problem hitting the remaining endpoints. The same load was spread across fewer servers, which led to a cascading failure from server to server.In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect had hit servers across the fleet and left them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.Several services, including Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and the Office apps, failed out of the faulty gateway infrastructure. That is why they were restored earlier. For most of the outage, Teams chats and meetings worked without issue. Not every service can do this, though. Exchange Online, for example, cannot fail out of this gateway.Recovery took longer because servers that came back into service were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again. Microsoft said its normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from such a broad unresponsive state.As the main defect was a latent bug from several months earlier, the company’s normal rollback, flighting and feature flags could not quickly undo the change.Once engineers confirmed the defect as the cause, they built an update that returned the code path to its previously known good state. To apply the fix and slowly bring the service back, they took groups of servers out of service, applied the change and restarted them before returning them to service. They did this carefully on large amounts of infrastructure at a time, such as 50% or more of a region.
Article Summary: Microsoft has apologised for a global outage that hit its Microsoft 365 services last week. The company has shared the Preliminary Post-Incident Report on the outage. According to Microsoft, three main factors came together to cause the global outage of the networking gateway that sits in front of many services. The first cause was a latent defect that left servers overwhelmed and unresponsive.

Article Title: California rejected Billionaire tax with 53 to 47 percent 'no' vote, 'lot thanks' to Sergey Brin; but 5 other states are preparing bills to bring new taxes for America's richest
Article Text:
Representative Image

What taxes five other states have or are planning for their richest

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why California’s billionaire tax faced opposition

California voters have recently rejected a proposed tax on billionaires. Proposition 40, which sought a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, lost by roughly 53% to 47% following a campaign financed by wealthy opponents, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin . The measure would have directed most proceeds towards healthcare, with additional funding for education and food assistance. Brin contributed more than $100 million to Building a Better California, a political committee opposing the proposal. However, California’s rejection comes as five other states have adopted taxes targeting the richest.Those measures differ from Proposition 40: they tax income above specified thresholds, rather than accumulated wealth such as shares and business holdings. Several are scheduled to take effect in 2027 or 2028, while others are already in place. Here’s what we know about these taxes:Massachusetts: Voters approved an additional 4% tax on income above $1 million in 2022, which became effective in 2023. The threshold rises with inflation and stands at $1,107,750 for the 2026 tax year. Revenue from this supports education and transportation in the state.Hawaii: A new top personal income-tax rate of 13% will take effect in 2027. For married couples filing jointly, that rate applies to income above $1 million. The state’s tax department estimates that the change will generate an additional $53 million in 2027. The 13% figure is the applicable tax rate, rather than an additional 13% surcharge.Maine: A 2% surcharge, which was set to start applying in 2027, has already taken effect in the 2026 tax year. It applies to taxable income above $1 million for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers, heads of household, and surviving spouses.Rhode Island: A surcharge on taxable income exceeding $1 million is set to begin at 1% in 2027, increase to 2% in 2028 and reach 3% in 2029. Once fully implemented, it raises the rate on income above that threshold from 5.99% to 8.99%.Washington: Lawmakers enacted a 9.9% tax on Washington taxable income above $1 million, which is set to begin January 1, 2028. The first returns and payments covering that income will be due in 2029.California Governor Gavin Newsom was among the Democrats opposing the measure. Critics claimed that it could encourage wealthy residents to leave, weakening the state’s income-tax base.Meanwhile, California’s Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated that the proposal could generate tens of billions of dollars over several years. It also warned of a possible continuing reduction of less than $1 billion annually in income-tax revenue as billionaires changed their behaviour. That was a potential fiscal consequence, rather than a confirmed loss.
Article Summary: California voters have rejected a proposed tax on billionaires. Proposition 40 sought a one-time 5% tax on their wealth. It lost by roughly 53% to 47% following a campaign financed by wealthy opponents, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin. But five other states have adopted taxes targeting the richest.

Article Title: How Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's resignation has shocked people in his birthplace, where he enjoys a Godlike status and is called 'the people's dad'
Article Text:
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang

Why Taiwan calls Jensen Huang ‘The People’s Dad’

Mixed feelings and conspiracy theories in Taipei

Why Huang’s resignation raises concerns over chip industry future

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jensen Huang resigned last week as Nvidia’s chief executive, and when news broke in Taiwan, people, including the hairstylist Ray Wang, were upset. For nearly a decade, Wang has cut Huang’s hair, watching it shift from salt-and-pepper to silver. Now, he is holding out hope for a comeback. “Maybe they’ll bring him back,” Wang said, “the way Apple brought back Steve Jobs.” According to a report, Wang’s reaction captures the shock and disbelief rippling across Taiwan following Huang’s sudden exit triggered by reports of affairs with an Nvidia executive and a businesswoman, Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials suspected of spying for China, an allegation Beijing has denied.Although Huang is an American citizen who moved to the US at age 9, he was born in Taiwan and holds a near-godlike status on the island nation. Whenever he visits, crowds mob him at night markets and line up for autographs. Local restaurants where he has eaten frame his photos on their walls like a Hollywood movie star.Hailed as the “pride of Taiwan” and affectionately nicknamed “the people’s dad,” Huang’s visits regularly spark a media and fan frenzy dubbed “Jensanity” – a play on the “Linsanity” craze that once surrounded Taiwanese-American basketball star Jeremy Lin, The New York Times reported.Since co-founding Nvidia in 1993, Huang made Nvidia’s bond with Taiwan deeply personal. Taiwan is home to TSMC, the chipmaking giant that produces roughly 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors and is driving the island’s projected 12% economic growth this year. Nvidia is TSMC’s biggest customer and Huang made sure to publicly credit the people building his chips and servers.Notably, that personal touch paid off in business. Huang flew to Taiwan last November when he needed TSMC to allocate more production capacity to Nvidia. He sat down for hot pot with senior executives and patiently signed whiskey bottles for factory employees. Chen noted that getting more chips out of a maxed-out factory requires managers to reshuffle schedules and staff to work overtime – something they might not have done so eagerly for other American tech giants that hadn't built the same goodwill.Across Taipei, many people feel Huang was treated harshly. Some observers have even floated conspiracy theories, speculating that American business and political leaders grew uneasy with the rising clout of executives of Taiwanese and Chinese descent and worked to force him out.“We felt the process didn’t seem quite fair. We felt it all happened too fast,” said Da-Xiang Hu, a local tech professional.Among semiconductor insiders, the report says, Huang’s departure has raised questions about who will guide the industry next. Citing a longtime semiconductor analyst, speaking anonymously, the publication says that modern AI wouldn’t exist without Nvidia. Suppliers had grown used to following Huang’s vision, trusting his instincts on where technology was heading even when it meant taking risks.Without him, the analyst wondered whose judgment those suppliers will trust.Just hours before Huang stepped down, Taiwan’s deputy minister of economic affairs, Chin-Tsang Ho, expressed hope that the transition wouldn't disrupt ties. “We hope things won’t change too much because he understands Taiwan better than anyone,” Ho said.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang resigned last week as Nvidia’s chief executive. He was born in Taiwan and holds a near-godlike status on the island nation. Whenever he visits, crowds mob him at night markets and line up for autographs.

Article Title: After asking employees to use AI, PwC now wants 85,000 of them to not trust AI blindly; the company's HR head says: We will continue to assess our people against...
Article Text:
File image: PWC (Reuters)

PwC’s critical thinking course begins by testing how employees think

Year-end performance reviews will measure the new skills

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

PwC is putting more than 85,000 partners and employees through a new certification in critical thinking and judgment, built to teach them when to push back on the AI tools the firm has spent years asking them to use. The programme starts in December and covers PwC’s US and Mexico offices along with its Acceleration Centers. Everyone is expected to finish by June 2027, the end of the firm’s fiscal year. The initiative is reportedly worth $100 million.The reasoning is practical. AI now handles much of the research, writing and analysis that junior staff once did by hand, and that repetitive work is where professionals used to build judgment. “As AI takes on more of these foundational tasks, some of the repetition that really helped our people to develop critical thinking and judgment just won’t be there,” said Yolanda Seals-Coffield, chief people and inclusion officer at PwC US.The shift is already showing. Seals-Coffield said first-year associates are doing different work than they did two years ago. A recent PwC analysis of US job listings found that entry-level roles exposed to AI were far more likely to ask for senior-level skills such as judgment and leadership than they were in 2019.The firm has drawn up 15 AI skills and 15 human skills, including empathy and adaptability, that it believes will set employees apart. This certification focuses on the two it considers vital.The certification runs for about six months and opens with a diagnostic that identifies a person’s thinking style. Some people instinctively question assumptions, some reflect, and others are pragmatists. The aim is to show where each person is strong and where they need work.From there, participants take classes developed with professors, including academics affiliated with Wharton and Harvard, and veteran PwC staff. Masterclass videos follow, then simulations tailored to each person’s work.Margaret Burke, PwC US’s leader of talent acquisition and development, gave the example of an AI model producing a tax analysis. Instead of accepting the result, employees learn to trace the model’s reasoning and check where it pulled its data from, then decide whether the conclusion holds up. “It’s an opportunity to practice the judgment involved in making a decision, rather than simply learning about critical thinking in theory,” she said.The final stage brings AI back in. A personalised AI coach will help staff apply the framework to daily work, whether that means rehearsing a difficult conversation, reviewing a proposal and anticipating questions before a client meeting or working out who on a team takes which role. Content will vary by seniority.There is no pass or fail exam. The idea, Seals-Coffield said, is “to give people these repeatable skills” and then assess them at year-end. Development leaders will evaluate that proficiency as part of PwC’s performance review process.PwC also plans to open its framework to any university in early 2027 and fund selected institutions to build it into introductory courses.The programme arrives as PwC widens its hiring. Seals-Coffield said the firm is hiring more engineers and technologists than ever, and they now work in its tax and assurance divisions too. It still makes offers to most summer interns, though it declined to share year-over-year entry-level hiring figures.Finishing the certificate won’t end the scrutiny. The AI coach will keep delivering new material as PwC sees fit. “We will continue to assess our people against their AI and human skills proficiencies throughout the course of their career,” Seals-Coffield said.
Article Summary: PwC is putting more than 85,000 partners and employees through a new certification in critical thinking and judgment. The programme starts in December and covers PwC’s US and Mexico offices along with its Acceleration Centers. The initiative is reportedly worth $100 million.
